'''Greenville''' is the southernmost section of [[Jersey City, New Jersey|Jersey City]] in [[Hudson County, New Jersey|Hudson County]], in the [[U.S. state]] of [[New Jersey]].<ref>[http://www.state.nj.us/infobank/localnames.txt Locality Search], State of New Jersey; accessed February 7, 2015.</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.destinationjerseycity.com/districts.php |title=Jersey City's Districts |access-date=2009-03-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080820073921/http://destinationjerseycity.com/districts.php |archive-date=2008-08-20 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Greenville">{{cite web |title=Greenville |work=Jersey City A to Z |publisher=New Jersey City University |url=https://www.njcu.edu/programs/jchistory/Pages/G_Pages/Greenville2.htm |access-date=2014-09-03 |archive-date=November 5, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141105064525/http://www.njcu.edu/programs/jchistory/pages/G_Pages/Greenville2.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |publisher=Hagstrom Map Company, Inc |isbn=978-0-88097-763-0 |title=Hudson County New Jersey Street Map |year=2008}}</ref>

==Geography==
[[File:Greenville Garfield JC jeh.JPG|thumb|upright|Welcome to Greenville]]
In its broadest definition, Greenville encompasses the area south of the [[West Side, Jersey City|West Side Branch]] of [[Hudson-Bergen Light Rail]] and north of the [[Curries Woods|city line]] with [[Bayonne, New Jersey|Bayonne]], between the [[Upper New York Bay]] and the [[Newark Bay]], and corresponds to the postal area [[ZIP Code]] 07305.

The central core of Greenville (between [[Bergen Point Plank Road|Garfield Avenue]] and [[West Side Avenue (HBLR station)|West Side Avenue]]) is primarily residential, consisting mostly of one- and two-family homes and lowrise apartment buildings. Principal thoroughfares include [[Martin Luther King Drive (Hudson County)|MLK Drive]], [[Old Bergen Road]] and [[Danforth Avenue (Hudson County)|Danforth Avenue]].

East of [[New Jersey Turnpike]] [[Newark Bay Bridge|Newark Bay]] Extension ([[Interstate 78 in New Jersey|Interstate 78]]) lie the [[Greenville Yard]], an intermodal facility,<ref>[http://www.panynj.gov/.../seaport/.../Regional_rail.html NY Harbor Intermodal Facilities] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20110612020831/http://www.panynj.gov/.../seaport/.../Regional_rail.html |date=June 12, 2011 }}, panynj.gov; accessed May 3, 2020.</ref> [[Port Jersey]], [[Port Liberté, Jersey City|Port Liberté]], (a [[gated community|gated residential community]]), and the Caven Point Section of [[Liberty State Park]]. Slightly further inland and parallel to the route of the Turnpike was the route of the [[Morris Canal]] until it was abandoned in the 1920s. A small (filled-in) portion of the canal still exists in [[Country Village, Jersey City|Country Village]],<ref>[http://jerseycityonline.com/morris_canal.htm Morris Canal] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101208101024/http://www.jerseycityonline.com/morris_canal.htm |date=December 8, 2010 }}, JerseyCityonline.com; accessed May 3, 2020.</ref> a neighborhood near [[Droyer's Point]] and the [[West Side, Jersey City|West Side]]. The [[Jackson Hill, Jersey City|Claremont Section]] straddles Greenville and [[Bergen-Lafayette, Jersey City|Bergen-Lafayette]].{{citation needed|date=May 2020}}

Greenville parks include Bayside Park, off Garfield Avenue, Audubon Park, a city square along [[John F. Kennedy]] Avenue, Fulton Avenue Park along [[Martin Luther King]] Drive, McGovern Park, Columbia Park, and [[Curries Woods|Mercer Park]], just north of [[Interstate 78]]. Cochrane Athletic Field is located near the [[Hudson Waterfront]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://everythingjerseycity.com/explore-jc/parks/|title = Parks}}</ref> In May 2020, construction started on Mary McLeod Bethune Park.<ref name = mary>{{cite web | url = https://jerseydigs.com/construction-starts-on-mary-mcleod-bethune-park-in-jersey-city/ | publisher = Jersey Digs | title =Construction Starts on Mary McLeod Bethune Park in Jersey City | date = 19 May 2020 | access-date = 27 September 2020}}</ref>

The [[Afro-American Historical and Cultural Society Museum]] is located at the Greenville Branch of the [[Jersey City Free Public Library]],<ref>[http://www.cityofjerseycity.org/docs/afroam.shtml Afro-American Historical Society Museum], cityofjerseycity.org; accessed May 3, 2020.</ref> Greenville Hospital, [[Henry Snyder High School]], and [[New Jersey City University]] all located on the district's main thoroughfare, [[County Route 501 (New Jersey)|Kennedy Boulevard]]. Greenville Hospital closed in 2008,<ref>[http://www.nj.com/jjournal-news/index.ssf/2012/08/jersey_city_medical_center_wil_1.html Jersey City Medical Center], nj.com; accessed May 3, 2020.</ref> was renovated, and is now part of [[Barnabas Health]] which operates [[Jersey City Medical Center]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rwjbh.org/our-locations/specialty-centers/jersey-city-medical-center-at-greenville/|title = New Jersey Health System}}</ref> Greenville is also home to historic [[Bayview – New York Bay Cemetery]], which includes a [[Commonwealth War Graves Commission|Commonwealth war grave]], of a [[World War I]] seaman and 1800s opera singer, [[Lillian Nordica]].

==History==

===Minkakwa, Kewan, and Pamrapo===
What became Greenville was the territory of the [[Hackensack (Native Americans)|Hackensack]] and [[Raritan (Native Americans)|Raritan]] [[Native Americans in the United States|Indian]]s at the time of European contact in the 17th century. They called the area on [[Bergen Neck]] ''[[Minkakwa]]'' (alternatively spelled ''Minelque'' and ''Minackqua'') meaning "a place of good crossing". This is likely so because it was the most convenient pass between the two bays on either side of the neck. Interpreted as "place where the coves meet", in this case where they are closest to each, it describes a spot advantageous for [[portage]].<ref>http://quod.lib.umich.edu/cgi/t/text/text-idx?c=moa&cc=moa&sid=95e3f6e828e116b80d4cccd93c806bc1&view=text&rgn=main&idno=AFJ8379.0001.001 page 50</ref> The area was first settled by [[New Netherlander]]s in 1647.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Klett |first=Joseph |title=An Account of East Jersey's Seven Settled Towns, circa 1684 |url=https://www.nj.gov/state/archives/pdf/pasevensettledtowns.pdf |journal=The Genealogical Magazine of New Jersey |volume=80 |issue=September 2005 |pages=106–114 |access-date=June 14, 2018}}</ref> The Caven Point settlement on the west shore of the [[Upper New York Bay]] between [[Pamrapo]] and [[Communipaw]] was part of [[Pavonia, New Netherland|Pavonia]], which, upon receiving its municipal charter in 1661 was renamed [[Bergen, New Netherland|Bergen]]. The name ''Caven'' is an [[anglicisation]] of the Dutch word ''Kewan'',<ref>{{citation |last=Ferretti |first=Fred |title=Jersey City Hopes to Save Caven Point |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 10, 1979 }}</ref> which in turn was a "[[Dutchification|Batavianized]]"<ref>{{cite book |last=Shorto |first=Russell |author-link=Russell Shorto |title=The Island at the Center of the World: The Epic Story of Dutch Manhattan and the Forgotten Colony that Shaped America |year=2004 |publisher=Random House |isbn=1-4000-7867-9}}</ref> derivative of an [[Algonquian languages|Algonquian]] word meaning "peninsula".<ref>{{cite book |last=Winfield |first=Charles |title=HISTORY OF THE COUNTY OF HUDSON, NEW JERSEY: ''From its Earliest Settlement to the Present Time'' |publisher=Kennaud & Hay Stationery M'fg and Printing Company |year=1874 |location=New York |page=51 }}</ref>

===Bergen, Greenville, Jersey===
[[File:GreenvilleJC1872map.tiff|thumb|Greenville in 1872, one year before consolidation]]
During the British and early American colonial era the area was part of [[Bergen Township, New Jersey (pre-1862)|Bergen Township]]. The 19th century [[Jersey City and Bergen Point Plank Road]] (today's Garfield Avenue) ran through Greenville (from [[Paulus Hook]] to [[Bergen Point]]). Greenville became part of the newly formed Hudson County in 1840. The town grew as a fashionable suburb of New York City.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1881/05/13/98556154.pdf |work=The New York Times |title=High Fares In Jersey.; Steps Taken By The Residents Of Greenville To Remedy Them |date=May 13, 1881}}</ref> [[Greenville Township, New Jersey|Greenville Township]] was incorporated as a [[Township (New Jersey)|township]] by an Act of the [[New Jersey Legislature]] on April 14, 1863, from portions of [[Bergen Town, New Jersey|Bergen Town]].<ref name=Story>"The Story of New Jersey's Civil Boundaries: 1606-1968", John P. Snyder, Bureau of Geology and Topography; Trenton, New Jersey; 1969. p. 146.</ref> It was absorbed into Jersey City on February 4, 1873, ending its life as an independent municipality.<ref name=Story/><ref>"Municipal Incorporations of the State of New Jersey (according to Counties)" prepared by the Division of Local Government, Department of the Treasury (New Jersey); December 1, 1958, p. 78 - Extinct List.</ref> Armbruster's Greenville Schuetzen Park on Hudson Boulevard opened in the 1870s.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://njcu.libguides.com/jerseycitypastandpresent/armbrustersschuetzenpark |title=Armbruster's Greenville Schuetzen Park - Jersey City Past and Present - Library Guides at New Jersey City University |website=njcu.libguides.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190602035839/https://njcu.libguides.com/jerseycitypastandpresent/armbrustersschuetzenpark |archive-date=2019-06-02}}</ref>

===20th century===
Greenville was settled by many working-class Irish Catholic families, as well as other ethnic groups. The area's demographics changed dramatically starting in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, with the decline of factories and the collapse of the independent railroad lines. The neighborhood east of Kennedy Boulevard was later settled by African Americans, while that west of Kennedy Boulevard is more diverse with a sizable [[Filipino Americans|Filipino]] population. Greenville also has a sizable Hispanic and [[Egyptians|Egyptian]] population, and many of the older Irish residents still remain in the neighborhood.{{citation needed|date=September 2014}}

===21st century===
[[File:AudubonPark.JerseyCity.jpg|thumb|left|Audubon Park]]
In 2005, [[Jersey City]] enacted a curfew for business owners on some of Greenville, including Martin Luther King Drive and Ocean Avenue.<ref>[https://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=F60B15FB3F5B0C758EDDAA0894DD404482&n=Top%2fReference%2fTimes%20Topics%2fSubjects%2fC%2fCrime%20and%20Criminals Jersey City Curfew Tackles Crime, but May Hit Profits, Too], ''The New York Times'', March 25, 2005</ref> On the [[West Side, Jersey City|West Side]] of Greenville, [[New Jersey City University]] unveiled plans for a $350 million expansion into the West Side neighborhood surrounding the university, including a performance art building with two theaters, retail stores, a restaurant, and student housing.<ref name = njcom>{{cite web |url=https://www.nj.com/hudson/2015/09/new_jersey_city_university_readies_for_350m_expans.html |publisher=NJ.com |title=Jersey City building boom coming to NJCU campus with $350M plan |date=3 September 2015 |access-date=4 June 2019}}</ref>

During the 2010s Greenville underwent a revitalization, with the return of long-term residents and businesses.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jerseydigs.com/gsecdcs-home-ownership-initiative-is-revitalizing-greenville/|title=GSECDC's Home Ownership Initiative is Revitalizing Greenville One Home at a Time|date=5 July 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130411043610/http://www.jerseycityindependent.com/2013/03/29/neighborhood-spotlight-greenville-community-in-progress/}}</ref> The section around [[Jackson Hill, Jersey City|Jackson Hill]] has seen considerable local and federal infrastructure spending.

The area is considered, relative to [[Manhattan]], [[Brooklyn]] and [[Queens]], to be an affordable part of the New York City region. A number of [[Ultra-Orthodox Jews]] and young Jewish and Hispanic families have purchased homes and built a growing community in Greenville.<ref name = newyorktimes2>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/08/02/nyregion/ultra-orthodox-jews-hasidim-new-jersey.html |work=The New York Times |title=Uneasy Welcome as Ultra-Orthodox Jews Extend Beyond New York |date=2 August 2017 |access-date=4 June 2019|last1=Berger |first1=Joseph }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=3yWMbrk_kQw |title=Orthodox Jews Arrive in Jersey City Neighborhood, Raising Hopes and Fears |website=m.youtube.com |access-date=December 11, 2019}}</ref> Since the mid-2010s Jersey City has experienced a rise in [[Hasidic Judaism|Hasidic Orthodox Jews]], who are moving to Greenville from [[Williamsburg, Brooklyn]], attracted by the relatively low housing price. While the relationship between the local [[African Americans|African American]] community and the Orthodox Jewish community is good, there have been complaints that Jewish buyers solicited them to sell their houses, prompting the city council to pass a no-knock ordinance that barred investors from going door-to-door.<ref name = newyorktimes2 /><ref>{{cite web |title=Orthodox Jews Arrive in Jersey City Neighborhood, Raising Hopes and Fears |url=https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=3yWMbrk_kQw |date=April 22, 2016 |access-date=December 11, 2019 |publisher=[[NJTV]]}}</ref> A [[kosher foods|kosher market]] in the community was the site of a [[shootout]] in the [[2019 Jersey City shooting]].<ref name = NYT12dec2019>{{cite web |last=Knoll |first=Corina |title=How 2 Drifters Brought Anti-Semitic Terror to Jersey City |work=The New York Times |date=December 15, 2019 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/15/nyregion/jersey-city-shooting-terrorism.html?action=click&module=Top%20Stories&pgtype=Homepage |access-date=December 15, 2019}}</ref><ref name = WSJ11dec2019>{{cite web |last1=De Avila |first1=Joseph |last2=Blint-Welsh |first2=Tyler |title=New Jersey Shooters Targeted Kosher Grocery Store, Jersey City Mayor Says |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |date=December 11, 2019 |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/new-jersey-gunmen-targeted-kosher-grocery-store-jersey-city-mayor-says-11576071931 |access-date=December 11, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last=Helfand |first=Zach |title=Untangling the Hate at the Heart of the Mass Shooting in Jersey City |magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |date=December 11, 2019 |url=https://www.newyorker.com/news/dispatch/untangling-the-hate-at-the-heart-of-the-mass-shooting-in-jersey-city |access-date=December 15, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Sales |first1=Ben |last2=Adkins |first2=Laura E. |title=Orthodox Jews tried to build a home in Jersey City. Then a shooting terrorized their community |publisher=[[Jewish Telegraphic Agency]] |date=December 11, 2019 |url=https://www.jta.org/2019/12/11/united-states/orthodox-jews-tried-to-build-a-home-in-jersey-city-then-a-shooting-terrorized-their-community}}</ref>

==Public transportation==
[[File:NJ Transit Flxible Metro-B 1712.jpg|thumb|NJT 81]]
The [[Richard Street (HBLR station)|Richard Street]] and [[Danforth Avenue (HBLR station)|Danforth Avenue]] stations of the [[Hudson-Bergen Light Rail]] are located on the district's east side east of [[Bergen Point Plank Road|Garfield Avenue]], while [[West Side, Jersey City|West Side Branch]] [[Hudson-Bergen Light Rail]] stations (including the [[Martin Luther King Drive (HBLR station)|MLK Station]]) are on its northern perimeter, which overlaps [[Bergen-Lafayette, Jersey City|Bergen-Lafayette]]. Several [[NJ Transit|New Jersey Transit]] bus routes serve this area. The [[NJ Transit bus garages|Greenville Bus Garage]] on Old Bergen Road houses more than 120 buses for several [[List of NJ Transit bus routes (1–99)|NJ Transit bus routes]].
